messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

He is 51 years old and works as a school principal, a role that has long suited him because he is organized, steady, and used to carrying other people’s concerns without making a scene of his own. Before the illness, he thinks of himself as healthy in a practical, unremarkable way. He gets through the demands of the school day, takes care of his home, and shares an easy, familiar life with his wife. Their routines are ordinary and comforting: coffee in the morning, brief conversations about the day ahead, plans for weekends that never feel urgent. He does not imagine that anything serious is coming.

The change begins with what first seems like a stubborn, nonspecific illness. He notices fatigue, a heaviness in his body, and a sense that something is off. At first, he pushes through it. He has spent years telling students and staff to keep going, and he does the same with himself. But the symptoms intensify, and eventually he is faced with the reality of a life-threatening medical crisis. The medical setting becomes the center of his world: appointments, tests, waiting rooms, fluorescent lights, conversations that start calmly and then become harder to follow. He remembers the exact tone in people’s voices when they explain what is happening, the careful pause before certain words, the way his wife’s face changes as the seriousness becomes clear.

He is frightened in a way he has never been before. He says that during the worst moments he feels as if his life narrows to breathing, monitors, and whether the next call will bring bad news. He tries to stay composed because that is his habit, but inside he feels raw and exposed. He notices how often he is thinking, “This is how it ends,” even when no one says it outright. His wife becomes both his anchor and, later, the person he loses in the wake of the illness. Her death leaves him not only grieving but also stunned by how quickly life can turn from ordinary to permanently altered. He carries the memory of her final days with painful clarity, and he describes them as if they are still happening somewhere just out of reach.

Since then, he moves through life with a sense that part of him remains in the hospital room and part of him is expected to function in the present. He returns to work because the school needs him and because structure helps him feel less untethered, but the role does not come easily anymore. He is still competent, still attentive, still able to manage crises involving students and staff, yet he notices that his concentration slips when the day grows quiet. A phone ringing unexpectedly can make his chest tighten. He startles more easily than he used to. When a child becomes ill at school or an ambulance passes nearby, he is flooded with images of his own hospitalization and his wife’s decline. He does not always see the images clearly, but he feels them in his body first: a surge of heat, a sinking sensation in his stomach, the urgent wish to get out of the room.

At home, he avoids the parts of the house that feel most connected to her. He leaves some belongings untouched for long stretches, then feels guilty for not being able to move them. Sleep is unreliable. He lies awake replaying conversations with doctors and imagining what he could have done differently, even when he knows on some level that the illness was not something he controlled. He wakes early with a tightness in his chest and begins the day already tired. There are moments when he is ashamed of how often he checks his own body for signs that something is wrong again. He reads medical information late at night, trying to make himself feel prepared, but ends up feeling more afraid.

He is not withdrawn in an obvious way; people at school still see him as composed and dependable. Yet those who know him well notice that he is quieter now, less likely to linger after meetings, less interested in the easy social exchanges he once handled with such ease. He says he feels split between the man others expect and the man who lives with the constant awareness that his body once failed him and that the person who knew him best is gone. Even now, he continues to work, to show up, to answer questions, to stand in hallways and attend events, but there is a guardedness in him that did not exist before. He lives carefully, always aware that the life he has now was built after a rupture he still cannot fully name without emotion rising in his throat.
